Exception Handling

　An exception is a so-called "exception" that is unexpected in normal processing, and in most cases can be thought of as the same as an "error".

Where Exceptions Occur

　Exceptions can occur anywhere in a program.
　Causing an exception is also called "throwing an exception".
　For example, suppose the following script causes an error.


Example:
    "3%0"!; // "Attempted division by zero" exception occurs

　While exceptions obviously occur in cases like this, there are also cases where it is not known whether one will occur or not.

Catching Exceptions

　You can catch exceptions by using the try keyword and the catch keyword.
　For example, to catch an exception that might occur as in the above example, you can write a script like the following:


Example:
    try // Because an exception might occur
    {
        func1(); // An exception might occur here
    }
    catch // Catch the exception
    {
        // This is executed when an exception occurs
        inform("Cannot load image."); // Display message
    }

　In this way, by writing processing that might cause an exception inside a try block, you can execute a catch block when an exception occurs. Error handling can be written cleanly like this.

　If no exception occurs in the try block, the catch block is not executed either.

　You can write anything inside a try block. As in this example, while there may be a clear possibility of an exception occurring on that line, even if an exception occurs deep inside nested function calls, if you have written try ... catch, you can return here at the point the exception occurs.

　When an exception occurs, the rest of the processing in the block is suspended, and execution returns to where the try statement is located.

　If another exception occurs inside the catch block, it will not be caught at this location. The exception will travel back up the function call stack, and if an exception is caught with try in another location, it will be caught there.

　It is also possible that another exception occurs between when an exception is thrown and when it reaches the catch block, but this behavior is undefined.

　If an exception is not caught anywhere within the script, it passes out of the script and is handed over to the application, where it is processed.

Note
Normally, such exceptions halt execution as errors, so it is recommended to write try ... catch in places where errors are likely to occur.

Exception Object

　Various information regarding the exception is thrown along with an object of the Exception class. This object is called an exception object. You can receive this with catch.
　For example, you can write a script like the following:

Example:
    try
    {
        loadImages("nothing.jpeg"); // Processing that might cause an exception
    }
    catch (e) // Receive the exception in the variable 'e'
    {
        // e.message represents the message string thrown with the exception.
        // This may explain the reason why the exception occurred.
        inform("Cannot load image.\n"+e.message);
    }
　In this way, by writing the receiving variable inside parentheses after catch, you can receive the exception object in that variable.
　The scope of this variable begins inside the block following catch and ends with this block. This variable does not need to be declared in advance.

throw Statement

　You can also throw exceptions. To throw an exception, use the throw keyword.
　For example, you can write a script like the following:

Example:
    function pow2(n)
    {
        // Calculates 2 to the power of n. n must be a positive integer.
        if(n<0) throw new Exception("Negative numbers cannot be specified.");
            // ^ Raises an exception
        return 1<<n;
    }
　If a negative number such as -1 is passed to the argument of this function, an exception occurs. The following statement throws the exception:


throw new Exception("Negative numbers cannot be specified.");

　Regarding new Exception("Negative numbers cannot be specified."), this creates an object of the Exception class using a string as an argument. Please refer to the Exception class for details. This newly created object is then thrown with the throw keyword.
　What can be thrown with the throw keyword is not limited to objects of the Exception class. You can also throw numbers, strings, or references to functions. However, throwing an object of the Exception class or a class derived from it is recommended. This is because when catching it, you only need to write the catch block assuming an Exception class object will arrive.

Rethrowing Exceptions

　In cases where an exception was caught in catch, but there may still be a try declared somewhere else that could receive the exception, you can rethrow the exception.
　For example, you can write a script like the following:

Example:
    function tryloadimage()
    {
        try
        {
            primaryLayer.loadImages("test1.bmp"); // Try reading test1.bmp
        }
        catch(e)
        {
            inform("Failed to load image.");
            throw e; // Display message, but rethrow exception
        }
    }

    function test()
    {
        // A function that calls tryloadimage and returns true if image loading succeeds,
        // otherwise returns false
        try
        {
            tryloadimage();
        }
        catch
        {
            return false;
        }
        return true;
    }
　Here, if test() is called and image loading fails, a message will be displayed by the inform method, but because the exception is thrown again, it can be caught by the catch inside the test function.
